fieldData.excerpt: Public incident report on the Radix Engine vault-authorisation vulnerability and loss of network liveness on 31 August 2026.
fieldData.main-content:
RADIX FOUNDATION

Public Incident Report
Radix Engine vault-authorisation vulnerability and loss of network liveness, 31 August
2026

 Field                        Detail

 Incident reference           RDX-INC-2026-0831

 Incident date                31 August 2026

 Report version               v1.4 17 September 2026

 Classification               Public — for distribution to the Radix community, validators, exchanges and
                              custodians

 Issued by                    Radix Foundation

 Status                       Contained. Root cause fixed. Network restoration in progress.




1. Executive summary
On 31 August 2026 an attacker exploited a previously undetected vulnerability in the Radix Engine,
the execution layer of the Radix network, to withdraw assets from third-party vaults without the
owners’ authorisation. The stolen assets were routed off the network through the Hyperlane bridge
and sold on external chains.
The vulnerability was not a bridge failure, a validator failure or a compromise of any user’s private
keys. It was a defect in how the Radix Engine enforced ownership of vaults when a vault reference
was passed into smart-contract code. That defect was introduced during a code tidy-up carried out
in June 2023 by RDX Works Limited, the Foundation’s contracted protocol development partner at
the time, and was not detected by the subsequent independent security audit conducted by Zellic in
August 2024.
Within approximately three hours of the first report, the Foundation, Hyperlane and members of the
Radix validator community had shut down the Hyperlane routes and, by taking sufficient validator
stake offline, deliberately broken the network’s liveness so that no further transaction could be
committed. This stopped any further exploitation. A fix to the Radix Engine and accompanying node
software has since been written, independently reviewed and tested by audit firms and other
trusted security parties. The matter has been reported to the States of Jersey Police and to UK law
enforcement, and the Foundation has supplied extensive forensic evidence.
This report sets out what happened, why, how it was contained, how it has been fixed, and what the
Foundation is doing to ensure a safe return to normal operation.


2. Background: audit history of the Radix Engine
The Radix Engine is the component of the Radix node that executes transactions and enforces the
ownership and access rules for every asset on the network. Its security history relevant to this
incident is as follows.

 Date                     Event

 Pre-June 2023            The Radix Engine was audited by Hacken and passed.

 June 2023                RDX Works development team carried out a routine code tidy up of the Radix
                          Engine. This change introduced the vulnerability described in Section 3.

 August 2024              The Radix protocol, including the engine kernel containing the vulnerability, was
                          audited by Zellic. The protocol passed with a high score for a Layer 1 protocol. The
                          vulnerability was not detected.

 31 August 2026           The vulnerability was identified and exploited by an external attacker.


The Foundation’s assessment, shared by the external forensic team, is that the attacker used AI-
assisted code-analysis tooling to locate the vulnerability in the publicly available Radix Engine source
code. The exploit was highly targeted and left a minimal footprint, which is consistent with
automated discovery followed by a deliberately engineered attack. The wider industry should expect
AI tooling to surface latent defects that conventional audits have missed; this is discussed further in
Section 9.


3. The vulnerability
3.1 Plain-language description
Every asset on Radix is held in a vault. A vault can only be withdrawn from by the account or
component that owns it. The Radix Engine is responsible for enforcing that rule.
The defect allowed a transaction to name any vault on the network by its internal address, pass that
address into a purpose-built piece of smart-contract code, and call the vault’s ordinary withdraw
function. The engine should have rejected the call because the caller did not own the vault. Because
of the defect, the engine treated the reference as if it were a normal, authorised reference and
permitted the withdrawal.

3.2 Technical summary
Internal vault addresses supplied in a transaction manifest are classified by the engine as “direct-
access” references, intended only for explicitly direct operations such as recall. When such a
reference was passed into a package call frame and the package then invoked ordinary methods
(get_amount and take) on the vault, the engine permitted those calls to proceed even though take is
not a direct-access method and should not have been callable through a direct-access reference. The
visibility check that should have blocked the ordinary method call did not recognise the borrowed
direct-access origin of the reference, so the withdrawal proceeded, subject only to the resource’s
withdrawer role, which is, correctly, set to allow all for ordinary transferable assets on the
assumption that vault ownership is enforced by the engine.
In summary: the exploit was carried out entirely by the attacker’s own package acting on the Radix
Engine. The Hyperlane package played no part in the exploit mechanism; it was used purely as the
destination to which the withdrawn assets were sent. The affected resources and their role
configurations were correct. The engine was not enforcing the ownership boundary those
configurations relied upon.

3.3 What was not affected
   • No user, validator or Foundation private keys were compromised.
   • Radix consensus operated correctly throughout, both in validly including the malicious
     transactions (which were not authorised by the vault owners) and, later, in ceasing to make
     progress once validator stake was taken offline.
   • The Hyperlane bridge, its validators and its message verification operated correctly. Every
     release on a destination chain matched a legitimately committed burn on Radix; the theft
     occurred on Radix before the bridge was used.
   • No admin, recall or clawback badge was used or abused.


4. Incident timeline
All times are UTC on 31 August 2026 unless stated. Local Jersey time (BST) is one hour ahead.

 Time (UTC)         Event

 16:02–16:57        Attacker executes 26 exploit transactions on Radix, withdrawing bridged assets from third
                    party vaults and dispatching them across the Hyperlane bridge to Ethereum, BNB Chain
                    and Solana.

 17:37              Community validators and Radix team members identify the unauthorised withdrawals and
                    escalate to Foundation leadership. Incident response initiated.

 17:53–18:09        Hyperlane removes Radix from its validator, relayer and scraper operations; Radix validator
                    infrastructure for the bridge scaled to zero by Hyperlane and its operators.

 18:09              SEAL 911 (the Security Alliance emergency response group) engaged to lead an
                    independent investigation. Foundation board briefed.

 18:11              Zellic engaged and begins investigation.

 18:35              Hyperlane asked to shut down the remaining Hyperlane routes for Radix assets.

 18:46              All market-making activity on centralised exchanges stopped by Foundation instruction;
                    exchanges asked to pause trading pending investigation.

 18:52              Hacken engaged and begins investigation.

 19:10–19:45        Foundation initiates and completes the multi signature transaction required to pause the
                    Ethereum route at the bridge level, providing an on chain containment layer independent
                    of the operator shutdown.
 Time (UTC)         Event

 ≈19:30             Initial findings from SEAL 911 and community researchers converge on a bug in the Radix
                    Engine’s vault authorisation logic.

 20:30              Emergency call convened between the Foundation, board members and key validators.
                    Determination that although bridged assets had been targeted for their external liquidity,
                    the vulnerability placed all assets on the network at risk. Decision taken to break network
                    liveness by taking a sufficient proportion of validator stake offline so that consensus could
                    no longer be reached.

 20:30–23:30        Network liveness broken through coordinated validator action; no further transactions
                    could be committed. Planning for fix and restoration begins.

 21:11              A third party developer engaged to begin work on a fix.

 1 Sep, 11:00       Candidate fix for the Radix Engine presented for review. Plan agreed for independent
                    verification and for the node software updates required to restore the network.

 2 Sep, 07:33       Crime report submitted to the States of Jersey Police.

 2 Sep, 07:47       Report submitted to UK police via Action Fraud.




5. Detection and containment
5.1 Detection
The unauthorised withdrawals were first noticed by members of the Radix community operating
validator nodes, who saw bridged assets being drained through the Hyperlane bridge. They
escalated immediately to the Radix team, which contacted Foundation leadership. The Foundation
established within minutes that the Hyperlane bridge itself was functioning correctly and that the
problem lay on the Radix side.

5.2 Shutting down the bridge
The Foundation contacted Hyperlane directly. Hyperlane disabled its Radix validator, relayer and
scraper operations and coordinated with its independent validator operators to take their Radix
signers offline. In parallel, the Foundation executed a multi-signature transaction to pause the
routes at the contract level. Together these steps ensured that no further Radix-originated bridge
messages could be delivered.

5.3 Breaking network liveness
Once the investigation established that the root cause was in the Radix Engine rather than in any
single application, it was clear that the bridged assets had been targeted simply because they had
liquidity on other chains; in principle, any vault on the network was exposed. The Foundation
convened an emergency call with key validators and board members and took the decision to stop
the network committing transactions.
The Radix network cannot be paused or switched off by any single party, and it was not halted in
that sense. Instead, validator node operators voluntarily and in coordination took sufficient stake
offline that the remaining validators could no longer reach the majority of stake that consensus
requires. Nodes continued to run and to attempt normal operation, but without enough stake
participating no further transaction could be committed: liveness was broken while the network
itself remained intact. This is the intended behaviour of a proof of stake network, consensus is
designed to stop rather than proceed without sufficient stake and it was the code doing exactly what
it is programmed to do that allowed the network to be protected. Liveness was lost within
approximately three hours of the initial report, and from that point no further transaction has been
committed.
The Foundation wishes to record its thanks to the community validators, SEAL 911, Zellic, Hacken
and Hyperlane, all of whom responded within minutes and worked through the night.

5.4 Other containment measures
   • All Foundation market making on centralised exchanges was stopped and exchanges were
     asked to pause XRD deposits, withdrawals and trading.
   • The malicious package, transaction manifests, receipts, affected vault lists and bridge operator
     logs were preserved for forensic analysis before any clean up activity.


6. Impact
The attacker withdrew Hyperlane-bridged representations of ETH, WBTC, USDT, USDC, BNB and SOL,
together with a small quantity of XRD used to pay transaction fees, from vaults owned by a number
of ecosystem packages and accounts, including liquidity pools. The assets that reached destination
chains were sold for ETH shortly afterwards. Although the attacker targeted bridged assets for their
liquidity on other chains, any package or account holding vaults was at risk.
Because network liveness was broken before the vulnerability could be applied more widely, the
Foundation is not aware of any unauthorised withdrawals beyond those identified in the timeline
above.


7. Remediation
7.1 The fix
A fix to the Radix Engine was developed within 48 hours of the liveness break. The fix enforces the
receiver capability before a method call frame is constructed: an ordinary method call on a vault is
now rejected when the caller holds only a direct-access reference, while intentional direct access
operations continue to work as designed. Defence in depth changes ensure that a direct access
reference retains that classification across borrows and cannot be used as an ordinary receiver by
any call path.
Regression tests have been added at both the unit level (proving the classification defect is closed)
and the integration level (proving that an unauthorised take on a third-party vault, with no intent
signers, is now rejected). Positive tests confirm that legitimate recall, and normal calls on owned and
global objects, are unaffected.

7.2 Node software updates
Applying the fix required a coordinated protocol upgrade of every validator node. Significant
additional engineering has been undertaken on the node software to allow the network to be
restarted safely from the state at which liveness was lost, to ensure that all nodes apply the
corrected engine at the same state version, and to prevent any transaction prepared against the
vulnerable engine from being executed after restart.

7.3 Independent verification
The Foundation has not relied on its own testing. The fix and the updated node software have been
reviewed and tested by the audit firms engaged during the incident and by other trusted parties. In
addition, a number of trusted security parties have independently deployed their own test networks
running the patched code and conducted their own adversarial testing against it.
Their collective conclusion is that, while no software can be guaranteed free of defects, no critical
security issues were identified in the patched Radix Engine or node software. The Foundation is
satisfied that the network can be safely restored on that basis.




8. Law enforcement
The Foundation has reported the incident as a crime to the States of Jersey Police and to UK police
through Action Fraud. Both have been supplied with extensive forensic evidence, including the
complete ledger of exploit transactions, the malicious package code, the attacker controlled
addresses on Radix and on each destination chain, the liquidation trail, and a full technical account
of the vulnerability and how it was introduced.
The Foundation will continue to cooperate fully with law enforcement and with any exchange or
analytics provider tracing the proceeds. Exchanges that receive or have received funds associated
with the attacker-controlled addresses are asked to contact the Foundation.


9. Root cause analysis and lessons learned
9.1 Root cause
The vulnerability was introduced in June 2023 during a routine code tidy up of the Radix Engine.
Three individually reasonable behaviours in the call frame reference model combined into an unsafe
path. The change was not caught by internal review at the time and was not detected by Zellic’s
independent audit in August 2024, despite that audit covering the kernel in which the defect sat.

9.2 Lessons
   • Refactoring is a security event. Code tidy ups and refactors of security critical components
     must be treated with the same rigour as new features: separate reviewers, explicit threat
     modelling of the reference and capability model, and a dedicated regression suite for
     authorisation boundaries.
   • Audits are necessary but not sufficient. Zellic, a well-regarded firm, audited this code and
     passed it. Audits sample; they do not prove. The Foundation recommends supplementing
  audits with continuous automated analysis, including AI-assisted review of the kind the
  attacker is believed to have used.
• External development must be evidenced. Where development of protocol code is
  outsourced, the contracting entity must evidence its change control, review and testing
  processes, and the Foundation, as the commissioning party, must retain independent
  verification capability rather than relying on the contractor’s assurance.
• RDX Works Limited. RDX Works Limited were informed of the situation and the root cause
  and have yet to respond.
• Coordinated halt capability worked and must be formalised. The network was halted by
  voluntary validator action within three hours. The Foundation will work with the validator
  community to document and rehearse this procedure so that it can be executed faster and
  with clearer authority in future.
